title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
author: Joel Becker · Nate Rush · Tom Cunningham · David Rein · Khalid Mahamud

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: METR provides adjacent evidence that AI may yield substantial but uncertain productivity gains and that autonomous agents require monitoring. However, the supplied material concerns technical workers and frontier-system evaluations, not legal workflows, verification by lawyers, or apprenticeship and competence risks, so it does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: ### Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity  A survey of 349 technical workers finds a median 1.4–2x self-reported change in value of work due to AI tools, expected to grow over time, though there are reasons to be skeptical of the magnitude.

*  ### Early Work on Monitorability Evaluations  We show preliminary results on a prototype evaluation that tests monitors' ability to catch AI agents doing side tasks, and AI agents' ability to bypass this monitoring.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: METR accepts that practical productivity must be measured through real workflows and materially develops the cluster’s methodological account by identifying participant- and task-selection biases as AI adoption spreads. It argues these effects likely make its estimate a lower bound, while acknowledging that the affected share limits the probable bias and that alternative designs introduce new trade-offs.
qs: -  **Developers have become more selective in which tasks they submit.** When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.
Together, these effects make it likely that our estimate reported above is a lower-bound on the true productivity effects of AI on these developers.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that task-level AI gains cannot be treated as general or realised productivity and materially extends the cluster by identifying adoption-driven selection bias, agentic concurrency, altered task choice, output-quality differences and noncompletion as threats to measurement. It also develops the cluster’s call for use-context-specific evaluation by proposing redesigned experiments and triangulation with observational, survey and time-use evidence.
qs: Altogether, these issues make it challenging to interpret our central estimate, and we believe it is likely a bad proxy for the real productivity impact of AI tools on these developers.
Due to the severity of these selection effects, we are working on changes to the design of our study.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on task context, actual usage and selection effects when interpreting measured productivity. It argues that selective participation and task withholding may make the experiment’s estimate a lower bound, while acknowledging that preferences and missing high-expected-uplift tasks do not directly measure gains or establish whole-job productivity.
qs: -  **Developers have become more selective in which tasks they submit.** When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.
Together, these effects make it likely that our estimate reported above is a lower-bound on the true productivity effects of AI on these developers.

kp.k: Later estimates suggest speedup but remain unreliable
kp.d: METR's software-development research update reports an early-2025 task-time increase of 19% (introduced as a 20% slowdown), using February–June 2025 data, with a confidence interval of +2% to +39%. In the study begun in August 2025, returning developers had an estimated task-time change of -18% (confidence interval -38% to +9%), and newly recruited developers -4% (-15% to +9%). Both later intervals include no effect. METR believes developers likely benefit more in early 2026, based on participant conversations, but describes its data as only very weak evidence about the increase's magnitude.
qs: Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%.
For the subset of the original developers who participated in the later study, we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%.
Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%.
However, because of the selection effects in our experiment, our data is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase.

kp.k: Task-randomized study covers experienced developers and diverse repositories
kp.d: The later study includes 57 experienced open-source developers, with median 10 years experience, across 143 repositories and 800+ tasks. Ten developers returned from the original study and 47 were newly recruited, including from smaller, more greenfield and less mature repositories. Participants received $50/hour, specified tasks before randomization into AI-allowed or AI-disallowed conditions, and recorded completion time for comparison.
qs: Developers were experienced open-source contributors with median 10 years experience. We have data from 57 developers, across 143 repos, and 800+ tasks.
Our second study, starting in August, consisted of 10 developers from the original study, plus a new set of 47 developers recruited from a more diverse set of open-source projects.
Each task was assigned to an “AI allowed” or “AI disallowed” condition.
The developers would record the amount of time it took to complete the task, and we could thus compare the average time required to complete a typical task with and without AI.

kp.k: AI adoption creates participant and task selection biases
kp.d: METR reports that wider adoption of agentic tools such as Claude Code and Codex during 2025 made recruitment and retention harder: more developers declined to work without AI for half their tasks. Surveys found 30% to 50% withheld some tasks because they did not want to perform them without AI. METR consequently believes its estimates likely understate productivity effects for these developers, while qualifying that selection appears to affect a minority of developers and tasks and that expected benefits are not measured benefits.
qs: Our study is thus systematically missing developers who have the most optimistic expectations about AI’s value.
When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.
Together, these effects make it likely that our estimate reported above is a lower-bound on the true productivity effects of AI on these developers.
The selection effects seem to affect a minority share of developers and of tasks, which limits the degree of bias.

kp.k: Reduced compensation likely contributes to selection
kp.d: METR attributes increased selection primarily to developers' higher expectations of AI-driven productivity gains, based on interviews and surveys. However, it also identifies the reduction in hourly compensation from $150/hour to $50/hour as a likely contributor, rather than attributing the change exclusively to AI capabilities.
qs: Based on our interviews and surveys we believe the increase in selection is primarily due to higher expectation of AI-driven uplift by our developers.
However the second study also had a lower pay rate, $50/hour instead of $150/hour in the original study, and this also likely contributed to the higher selection.

kp.k: Participant accounts illustrate selection, not verified productivity gains
kp.d: A newly recruited developer described avoiding tasks they expected AI to finish in 2 hours versus 20 hours manually. METR presents such accounts as evidence of task-selection mechanisms, not validated speedup estimates, and explicitly cautions that developers' self-reported gains can be unreliable.
qs: I avoid issues like AI can finish things in just 2 hours, but I have to spend 20 hours. I will feel so painful if the task is decided as AI-disallowed.
Some developers self-report very high speedups, though as we documented in our earlier study those estimates can be quite unreliable.

kp.k: AI changes task choice and output quality
kp.d: Some participants reported choosing different tasks to exploit agentic AI's strengths. METR argues this can make study tasks unrepresentative of work outside the experiment and prevent time differences from representing value differences. Participants also reported differences between conditions in subjective code quality and the documentation or tests produced; the document does not establish a uniform direction or magnitude of these quality differences.
qs: Some developers told us the types of tasks they attempted were different with agentic AI, leaning on the strengths of AI.
the time-differences within the study may not represent value-differences, due to the substitution in task-type.

Some developers told us the quality of the final work, for a given task, was different between AI-allowed and AI-disallowed conditions, e.g. differences in subjective code quality, or the amount of documentation or tests they chose to create.

kp.k: Noncompletion and concurrent agents complicate time measurement
kp.d: METR reports lower completion propensity for some tasks assigned to the AI-disallowed condition, including one developer who completed none of that condition's tasks. Some participants also struggled to record task time when working on unrelated tasks while agents ran. Together with selection and output differences, these issues lead METR to regard the central estimate as likely a poor proxy for real productivity impact.
qs: One developer did not complete any of the tasks that were assigned to the AI-disallowed condition.

Some developers reported it was challenging to report time-spent in completing tasks when they used agentic tools, because they would often work an unrelated task while waiting for the agent to complete its work.
Altogether, these issues make it challenging to interpret our central estimate, and we believe it is likely a bad proxy for the real productivity impact of AI tools on these developers.

kp.k: Alternative experiments trade compliance against realism and statistical power
kp.d: METR plans to explore shorter, intensive experiments and possibly higher pay to improve compliance, as well as fixed-task experiments rather than developer-selected tasks. It also considers randomizing developers to always or never use AI: this could alleviate task-level selection but worsen developer-level selection and reduce power to detect productivity effects. These are proposed designs, not demonstrated remedies.
qs: The selection issues would be alleviated if we had higher compliance, which could be achieved if we run shorter intense experiments, and possibly pay higher rates.
We could revert to a simpler design in which developers are given a fixed task to complete, either with or without AI assistance.
This alleviates some of the task-level selection problems, however it makes the developer-level selection problems worse, and has lower power in detecting productivity effects.

kp.k: Complementary measurement will track use, time and autonomous capability
kp.d: METR identifies developer productivity as an input to AI R&D acceleration and plans complementary observational research, carefully designed questionnaires with time-use studies, and evaluations of agents' autonomous task completion. It acknowledges biases in self-reported productivity counterfactuals and treats agent capability evaluations as relevant to productivity rather than equivalent to measured workplace effects. METR expects advancing capabilities to require continued redesign of measurement methods.
qs: The impact of AI tools on developer productivity is an important input to AI R&D acceleration
We intend to continue observation of our pool of open-source developers to understand how AI is used.

Despite the difficulty of interpreting self-reported productivity counterfactuals, and thus their potential biases, we are optimistic that careful choice of survey questions, along with time-use studies, could produce useful signals.
METR is continuing to build task evals, to measure the ability of agents to autonomously complete tasks, which has a clear relevance to productivity effects of agent adoption.
As model capabilities continue to increase, we expect to continue to need to redesign some portions of our capability and measurement techniques.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: METR reports a shift from measured developer slowdown in early 2025 toward possible speedups in its later experiment, but does not regard the later estimates as reliable measures of current productivity effects.
pts.d: This is a software-development source, not a claim about legal services. The METR authors report that their early study found AI increased task completion time by 19%. In the later study, the estimated change in completion time was −18% for returning developers and −4% for newly recruited developers. Based on participant conversations, the authors believe AI likely speeds developers up more in early 2026 than in early 2025, while explicitly treating the evidence for the magnitude as very weak. They also claim wider adoption of agentic tools changes participation, task selection and workflows, undermining task-level measurement. Some participants report choosing different tasks, producing different work quality or quantities of tests and documentation, and doing other work while agents run. These are reported workflow differences, not established improvements in quality.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines randomized task-level experiments with participant interviews and surveys, while identifying substantial selection and measurement problems in the later experiment.
pts.d: The later experiment includes 57 experienced open-source developers, 143 repositories and more than 800 tasks; 10 developers returned from the original study and 47 were newly recruited. Developers specified tasks before random assignment to AI-allowed or AI-disallowed conditions and recorded completion time. Both later estimates have confidence intervals spanning no effect. Interviews and surveys underpin the authors' interpretation that developers and tasks with high expected AI benefits are disproportionately absent: 30%–50% of developers reported withholding some tasks because they did not want to perform them without AI. The authors also identify lower compensation, differential task completion, output differences and difficulty recording time during concurrent agent use. They warn that self-reported large speedups can be unreliable. An unnamed participant's example of two hours with AI versus twenty without is a personal counterfactual illustrating selection, not an experimentally established tenfold gain.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The comparison is between February–June 2025 data and a follow-up begun in August 2025, interpreted in February 2026; future measurement difficulties are predicted to grow with capabilities and developer expectations.
pts.d: Published February 24, 2026, the article compares the original early-2025 experiment with a later experiment using the latest tools. The authors regard selection as likely biasing estimated benefits downward, but qualify this by noting that it appears to affect a minority of developers and tasks. Their suggested lower-bound interpretation is an inference, not a demonstrated numerical bound. Compensation fell from $150 to $50 per hour, which they acknowledge likely contributed to selection. They predict that increasing capabilities and expectations will further limit the existing design's validity. Proposed alternatives—including shorter intensive experiments, fixed-task studies, observational data, questionnaires and developer-level randomization—are research plans, not completed evidence of productivity gains.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate subjects are experienced open-source contributors, especially active agentic-AI adopters; the measurement implications also affect researchers studying developer productivity and AI R&D acceleration.
pts.d: Participants worked on their existing open-source projects and had a median of 10 years' experience. Newly recruited developers came from a more diverse repository pool, including smaller, greener and less mature projects. According to METR, developers most optimistic about AI are less willing to accept AI-disallowed work, and tasks expected to benefit most are more likely to be withheld. Consequently, the most active adopters may be underrepresented. Agent users' concurrent workflows complicate attribution of time to individual tasks, while changes in task mix mean time savings may not correspond to changes in output value. METR identifies developer productivity as relevant to AI R&D acceleration, but makes no specific prediction about legal professionals, legal markets or employment displacement.
